slide.title: Forecast Risk, Offer Support
slide.body: Icon of an appointment calendar with empty slots, an umbrella over one slot and a small bus icon. Small tag: AI in Healthcare · Lesson 6 · synthetic data.

scenes.voiceover: Every missed appointment is a lost chance to care for someone, and an empty slot another patient could have used. A model can predict who is likely to miss a visit. The harder question is what you do with that prediction.

slide.title: Operational AI
slide.body: Scheduling · Missed-appointment prediction · Bed management · Supply planning · Documentation support that clinicians review (see L08)

scenes.voiceover: Welcome to week two. Last week, we learned how clinical AI is built and judged. Now we turn to operations. Operational AI supports how a hospital or clinic runs. Common uses are scheduling, predicting missed appointments, managing beds, planning supplies, and drafting documents that clinicians review and sign.

slide.title: Same prediction, opposite effect
slide.body: Prediction: patients who live far away miss more visits. Left (red): overbook their slots → longer waits, sent home. Right (green): transport support or phone consultation.

scenes.voiceover: These tools do not make clinical decisions, but they still affect patients. Suppose a model finds that people who live far away miss more appointments. One clinic might overbook their slots, so if they do arrive, they wait longer or are sent home. Another clinic offers transport support or a phone consultation. Same prediction, opposite effect on equity.

slide.title: Linked is not caused
slide.body: Distance → missed visit, with a dashed arrow and a question mark. Hidden factors behind distance: cost · work hours · transport. Staff icon: interpret before acting.

scenes.voiceover: There is a second point. A factor linked with missed appointments is not proof that it causes them. Distance may stand in for cost, work hours or poor transport. Staff who know the community should interpret the pattern before choosing any action.

scenes.stock_query: outdoor market stalls under rain shelters
scenes.voiceover: Here is a simple way to picture it. A missed-appointment model is like a weather forecast. A forecast of rain does not tell you to cancel the market. It tells you to bring shelter. A good clinic uses a risk forecast to prepare support, not to shut people out.

scenes.stock_query: clinic manager talking with data analyst
scenes.voiceover: Let's see this on screen. Rosa Quispe manages a hypothetical outpatient clinic in Cusco, Peru. Many patients miss follow-up visits. She asks a data analyst to explore a synthetic dataset of two thousand appointments, shaped like her clinic's data.

screen_steps: Open the course notebook missed_appointments_synthetic.ipynb in Google Colab and sign in with a Google account.
Point out the first text cell: all data is generated by the code, and no real patient data is uploaded.
Choose Runtime, then Run all, and wait until every cell shows output.
scenes.voiceover: We open the course notebook in Google Colab and sign in with a Google account. The first text cell says that all the data is generated by the code, and no real patient data is uploaded. Then we choose Runtime, and Run all.

screen_steps: Scroll to the Step 2 code cell and highlight the lines that create distance_band and group by distance_band, reminder_sent and age_group.
Highlight the first output line: (2000, 6) missed rate: 0.304.
scenes.voiceover: We scroll to the Step two output. The code groups patients into distance bands, then prints the missed rate for each distance band, for reminder sent or not, and for each age group. Remember, these are synthetic numbers. Overall, about thirty percent of appointments were missed.

screen_steps: Highlight the distance_band table: 0-5 is 0.222, 5-15 is 0.267, 15-30 is 0.403, 30+ is 0.562.
Highlight the reminder_sent table: 0 is 0.400, 1 is 0.208.
Highlight the age_group table: 18-39 is 0.305, 40-64 is 0.303, 65+ is 0.306.
scenes.voiceover: Look at distance. Patients living more than thirty kilometres away missed fifty-six percent of visits, compared with twenty-two percent for those within five kilometres. Patients who received a reminder missed twenty-one percent, compared with forty percent without one. And age group made almost no difference.

screen_steps: Scroll to the logistic regression output.
Highlight the coefficients: distance_km 0.051, lead_days 0.031, reminder_sent -1.021, previous_missed 0.510.
Point to the positive values, then to the negative reminder_sent value.
scenes.voiceover: Finally, the notebook shows a simple logistic regression. Positive values go with more missed appointments, and negative values with fewer. Distance, days of waiting and previous missed visits are positive. Sending a reminder is clearly negative. These are associations in synthetic data, not causes.

slide.title: Rosa's decision
slide.body: Rejected (red cross): overbook distant patients. Proposed (green ticks): 1. reminders for every booking in Spanish or Quechua · 2. phone or video follow-up for distant patients, with transport support for in-person visits.

scenes.voiceover: Rosa reads the results with her team, and they talk about what the numbers might mean for their patients. She rejects the idea of overbooking distant patients. Instead, she proposes reminders for every booking, in Spanish or Quechua as the patient prefers, and a phone or video option for follow-up visits for patients who live far away, with transport support when an in-person visit is needed.

scenes.on_screen_text: A risk score is not a decision
scenes.voiceover: She plans to measure missed-visit rates by distance band after three months. A common mistake is to treat a risk score as a decision, and automatically overbook or cancel. Decide the action with staff and patients, and check whether it reduces differences between groups.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Operational AI: scheduling, no-shows, beds, supplies, documentation. 2. A prediction is not a cause or a decision. 3. Use predictions to offer support, not to penalise.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, operational AI supports scheduling, missed-appointment prediction, bed and supply planning, and documentation that clinicians review. Second, a prediction is not a cause, and it is not a decision. Staff who know the community should interpret it. Third, use predictions to offer support, not to penalise groups who already face barriers.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will run the same notebook, copy the missed rates for each factor, and propose two fair actions, plus one action you would not take. No coding is needed. It takes about thirty minutes. In the next lesson, we look at AI for patient engagement. See you there.
